Othello. The tragedy by William Shakespeare, written around 1603 or 1604, that depicts the moral destruction of a Moorish general in Venice, undone by the manipulations of his ensign Iago. The play is a masterwork of psychological warfare. Iago, passed over for promotion in favor of Cassio, harbors a consuming resentment and schemes to destroy Othello out of what he admits is motiveless envy and possible racist contempt. His weapon is language and psychology. He plants false evidence, makes insinuations, and asks leading questions that allow Othello to construct his own narrative of infidelity. Desdemona, a Venetian noblewoman, has married Othello in secret against her father's wishes, defying social convention. Iago targets her as the mechanism of Othello's destruction.

Othello's tragic flaw is not pride or ambition but a vulnerability to suggestion and an internalized doubt about his own worthiness. As a non-European character in the Venetian army—a fact the play exploits to devastating effect—he internalizes Iago's suggestions that he does not truly belong. Iago weaponizes Othello's own insecurity about being an outsider, and the general's noble character and love gradually corrode into murderous paranoia. At the play's center is the handkerchief, a token of love that Iago manipulates into false evidence of infidelity. This simple object drives the entire tragedy.

The play culminates in Othello's murder of Desdemona in a jealous rage, followed immediately by his realization of her innocence and his suicide. Othello stands as Shakespeare's most penetrating exploration of how prejudice, jealousy, and the power of suggestion can unravel even the most dignified person. The work stands alongside Hamlet, King Lear, and Macbeth as one of Shakespeare's four great tragedies, though Othello is distinguished by its focus on psychological destruction through manipulation rather than through external action or supernatural compulsion.
